items.stimulus: For decades, relief printmakers have cleaned ink from their carved blocks with mineral spirits, a solvent that removes oil-based ink quickly. mineral spirits have a drawback in some studios that the oil-and-soap method avoids.
mineral spirits should be banned from every printmaking studio regardless of its size.
students should give up relief printing in favor of techniques that use no ink at all.
items.explanation: Ruiz recommends a new cleaning method and gives one reason: mineral spirit fumes linger in small, poorly ventilated studios. the presence of observers can cause some species to be undercounted.

regarded earlier folklorists' catalogs as containing no useful information.

items.stimulus: Many conservation groups judge the health of a seabird colony by counting its nesting pairs each spring. Ecologist Tomás Reyna's team, however, spent three seasons also weighing chicks just before they fledged. The researchers argued that a colony can hold its nest count steady even as food shortages leave young birds too light to survive their first winter. The team's approach suggests that the researchers did NOT assume that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: a chick's weight at fledging can affect its chances of surviving the winter.
the food available to a colony can influence how its chicks develop.
a colony's health can decline without any change in its nest count.
a steady number of nesting pairs reliably shows that a colony is thriving.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the popular method of counting nests and then undercuts it. C.why: This is the researchers' central argument, nearly word for word. You may have read it as the 'corrected view' and picked it, but the blank asks for the view they did NOT hold.

When the park service commissioned a replacement, cartographer Ines Halvorsen insisted on 10-meter contours for the steep eastern trails. finer contours would reveal detail that matters on the eastern trails.

the old map's spacing hid terrain features that matter on some trails.

items.stimulus: Observational studies have long linked higher blood levels of vitamin D to fewer bone fractures, yet several large trials that gave vitamin D supplements to broad samples of adults found no reduction in fractures. Rather than conclude that the supplements are ineffective, nutrition scientist Priya Raman designed a new trial that enrolled only adults whose blood vitamin D fell below the deficiency threshold at the outset. Raman's design suggests that, in her view, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: vitamin D supplements cannot reduce fracture risk in adults whose blood levels are already above the deficiency threshold.
the link found in observational studies reflects other habits of adults with high vitamin D rather than the vitamin itself.
the earlier trials may have included too many adults who had little to gain from taking additional vitamin D.
the earlier trials demonstrated that supplements reduce fractures only in adults whose blood vitamin D was initially deficient.
items.explanation: Start with why Raman would run the trial this way. She refuses to read the earlier null results as proof that supplements fail, and she then enrols only deficient adults. That choice only makes sense if she thinks any benefit shows up mainly in deficient people, so a broad sample full of people who already had enough vitamin D could have hidden a real effect. Choice C states that belief. Its 'may' also fits the evidence: she is testing an explanation, not asserting one she has already proven.

A.why: You saw the key point, that the benefit is concentrated in deficient adults, and then took it one step too far. Raman's design only needs her to think adequate-level adults gain less, so including them would weaken the signal. It doesn't need her to think they gain nothing. 'Cannot' is strength creep.

B.why: You gave Raman a belief that her own action argues against. If she thought the observational link came from other habits and not from vitamin D, she would have no reason to run another supplement trial. The passage also says she specifically declined to conclude that the supplements are ineffective.

D.why: You turned Raman's hypothesis into a finding of the earlier trials. Those trials found no reduction in fractures, and nothing says they compared deficient and non-deficient adults. The idea that deficiency matters belongs to Raman's new design, not to their results.

items.stimulus: Print historians have often ordered the undated impressions of a single etched plate by the sharpness of their lines: because each pass through the press wears the copper slightly, crisper impressions were assumed to be earlier. Studying the etchings of the nineteenth-century printmaker Odile Ferrant, historian Ana Kovač noted that Ferrant's workshop periodically re-bit worn plates in acid, deepening their lines. Kovač therefore set line sharpness aside and ordered Ferrant's impressions by the dated watermarks in their paper. Kovač's approach suggests that she regarded ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the dated watermarks as a less dependable guide than line sharpness to the order of Ferrant's impressions.
a crisp impression from one of Ferrant's plates as possibly later than a faint impression from that plate.
impressions pulled after one of Ferrant's plates was re-bitten as crisper than those pulled when it was new.
line sharpness as uninformative about the order of the impressions from any etched plate of the nineteenth century.
items.explanation: Ask why Kovač dropped line sharpness. The old method depends on lines only ever getting fainter over time. Re-biting deepens worn lines, so an impression pulled after re-biting can look crisp even though it came late. For that reason Kovač can't trust 'crisper means earlier' for Ferrant's plates, which means she must accept that a crisp impression might come after a faint one. Choice B says exactly that, and 'possibly' keeps it as strong as the passage allows and no stronger.

A.why: You reversed the comparison. Kovač gave up line sharpness and used watermarks instead, so she must think watermarks are the more dependable guide for Ferrant's work, not the less dependable one.

C.why: You understood that re-biting restores crispness, then added a step the passage never takes. 'Deepening their lines' only means re-bitten plates are crisper than they were when worn. Nothing says they become crisper than the plate was when new, and Kovač's method doesn't depend on that comparison.

D.why: You stretched one workshop's practice into a rule about every plate. Kovač's reason for dropping line sharpness is specific to Ferrant, whose workshop re-bit its plates. Her approach says nothing about plates that were never re-bitten, and 'any' goes well past what she needs to believe.

items.stimulus: Some ecologists credit the return of wolves to a western valley with the recovery of its streamside willows, reasoning that wolves deter elk from browsing there. Ecologist Hana Ostrowski fenced willow plots to exclude elk entirely. Fenced willows outgrew unfenced ones overall, but at sites where the stream had cut a deep channel, fenced willows grew far less than fenced willows elsewhere. Ostrowski then began measuring groundwater depth at every site, suggesting she suspected that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: elk browsing had little effect on willows at deep-channel sites, where a shortage of water was the only factor limiting their growth.
elk avoided browsing at the deep-channel sites because the willows growing there had already been weakened by low groundwater.
the return of wolves had done nothing to aid willow recovery in the valley, whatever the depth of its stream channels.
keeping elk away might not be enough to restore willows where channel cutting had lowered the water available to their roots.
items.explanation: Hold two results together. First, fencing helped willows overall, so browsing matters. Second, fenced willows at deep-channel sites still grew poorly, so removing elk wasn't enough there. Measuring groundwater shows that Ostrowski suspected water as the other limit. D keeps both results: excluding elk 'might not be enough' at those sites. It doesn't say elk don't matter.

A.why: You noticed water and dropped elk. The data compare fenced plots with other fenced plots, not fenced with unfenced plots at deep-channel sites. Nothing shows that browsing had little effect there or that water was the 'only' factor.

B.why: This makes up a link between groundwater and how elk behave. The fences kept elk out entirely, so the poor growth inside them can't be explained by where elk chose to feed.

C.why: This goes much too far. Fenced willows outgrew unfenced ones, so reducing browsing does help, and that is the very mechanism the wolf explanation depends on. Her follow-up adds a second factor. It doesn't throw out the first.

items.stimulus: Editors of Antonín Halbich's Second Quartet have long printed the pencil revisions in his autograph score as his final intentions, since the score remained in his possession until his death. Musicologist Irena Vos compared the handwriting of each revision both with samples from Halbich's letters and with pages known to be written by the copyist who lived in his household during his last years. Vos's method suggests that in her view ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the score's remaining in Halbich's possession did not guarantee that every revision in it was written in his own hand.
the copyist had altered the quartet without Halbich's knowledge during the years the two shared a household.
even revisions in Halbich's own hand should be treated as less authoritative than the original ink text of the score.
the handwriting in Halbich's letters was too inconsistent to serve as a reliable basis for any comparison.
items.explanation: The editors reason that because Halbich kept the score, the revisions are his. Vos checks each revision against two hands, his and the copyist's. She would only do that if keeping the score didn't settle who wrote in it. A states that assumption. B.why: Even if the copyist wrote some revisions, they might have been taking Halbich's dictation. Handwriting can show who held the pencil, not whether Halbich knew. You gave her a belief that her method couldn't test and didn't need.

C.why: Vos questions who wrote the revisions, not whether Halbich's own changes count. If a revision is in his hand, nothing in her method would downgrade it.

D.why: She used the letters as her sample of Halbich's handwriting. She could only do that if she trusted them, so this choice reverses her reasoning.

items.stimulus: A regional museum attributes nine nineteenth-century quilts to a single maker because all nine contain the same printed cottons. Textile historian Joan Pell, noting that quilters in the region routinely traded fabric scraps, has recommended that the attribution be reassessed using measurements of stitch length and thread tension instead. Pell's recommendation implies that she believes ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the nine quilts were in fact made by several different quilters who had traded scraps of the same printed cottons.
the fabrics in a quilt are more likely than its stitching to reveal which quilter in the region made it.
a maker's stitching is more likely than a quilt's fabrics to distinguish that maker's work from the work of others nearby.
stitch length and thread tension remain identical across every quilt that a single maker ever produces.
items.explanation: Pell gives a reason why shared fabric is weak evidence: fabric moved between quilters. Then she proposes stitching instead. That recommendation only makes sense if she thinks stitching tells makers apart better than fabric does. C states that comparison in the right direction and doesn't claim that stitching is a perfect fingerprint.

A.why: You correctly saw that she distrusts the evidence, then treated that as her verdict. She asked for the quilts to be reassessed, which means she thinks the attribution is unproven, not that it's wrong.

B.why: This turns her comparison around. She is replacing fabric evidence with stitch evidence, so she must rank stitching higher.

D.why: Look at 'identical' and 'every.' Her method only needs one maker's stitches to vary less than different makers' stitches do. Perfect consistency is far more than she needs to assume.

items.stimulus: Because a tale about a drowned church bell is told in nearly identical form in dozens of Baltic coastal villages, folklorists long assumed that its versions descend through oral retelling from a single medieval original. When folklorist Aino Repo recorded the tale in 2019, she asked each teller not only from whom they had learned it but also whether they had ever read it in an 1871 anthology once sold widely along that coast. Repo's questions suggest that she thought ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the tale had not been told in the coastal villages at all before the 1871 anthology carried it into wide circulation.
the close agreement among the villages' versions might stem partly from a shared printed source, not from oral descent alone.
the anthology's compiler had probably assembled the printed text from versions told in those same coastal villages.
tellers who had read the anthology would tell the tale less faithfully than those who learned it only by ear.
items.explanation: The old view uses the near-identical versions as evidence of oral descent from one original. items.stimulus: The seismic hazard map for the city of Tarvel is based on the 150 years of earthquakes recorded by instruments and in written accounts, none stronger than magnitude 5.8. Seismologist Delia Moretti has recommended that the map be revised to incorporate excavations across the region's faults, where layers of offset sediment preserve evidence of ruptures thousands of years old. Moretti's recommendation implies that she believes ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the 150-year record exaggerates Tarvel's hazard by including moderate earthquakes that the prehistoric ruptures show to be rare.
an earthquake stronger than magnitude 5.8 is likely to strike Tarvel sooner than the current hazard map would predict.
the instrument records and written accounts are too unreliable to contribute anything to an accurate hazard map.
the region's largest earthquakes may occur too rarely to appear in 150 years of records, so the map could understate the hazard.
items.explanation: Why would anyone add evidence thousands of years old to a map built on 150 years? Because some events may happen less often than once in 150 years, so the current record could miss them. The record tops out at 5.8, so missing those events would make the map too low. D gives that reason and keeps the hedges 'may' and 'could.'

A.why: This reverses the direction of the error. She is reaching back in time for events the recent record leaves out, which would raise the estimated hazard, not lower it.

B.why: You correctly read 'the map may be too low' and then added timing. A longer record tells you what is possible, not when it will happen. Nothing she recommends predicts that a large earthquake is coming soon.

C.why: She asked for the excavations to be incorporated, meaning added to the existing record, not substituted for it. She thinks the record is too short, not that it is worthless.

items.stimulus: At the Neolithic site of Kerem Tal, flint sickle blades become roughly four times as common in layers dated after 7000 BCE, a change often cited as the start of intensive cereal farming there. Yet charred cereal grains in those same layers occur no more often than before. Archaeologist Ruth Adeyemi has begun examining the blades under a microscope for wear patterns that indicate which kinds of plants they cut, suggesting that in her view ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the rise in sickle blades might reflect more cutting of plants other than cereals rather than more cereal harvesting.
the blades were used chiefly for cutting reeds and wild grasses, so cereal farming at the site remained minor.
the charred grains preserved in those layers probably undercount how much cereal the site's residents ate.
a rise in cereal farming at the site after 7000 BCE led its residents to need many more flint blades.
items.explanation: The evidence splits: sickles rose, but cereal grains stayed flat. Adeyemi chose to check what the sickles cut. That makes sense only if she thought the blades might have been used on something besides cereal. A states that possibility and keeps it a possibility.

C.why: This would explain the split in a different way, but her action doesn't depend on it. If she thought the grain counts were the problem, she would study how grain is preserved, not wear on the blades.

D.why: This is the popular view that the flat grain counts undercut. Her test exists because she doubts that more sickles means more cereal farming, so choosing it gives her the opposite of her view.
